title: Double circulation: engineer the route
subtitle: Trace a blood journey, test a valve and calculate a pump output
objective: Explain how heart structure supports double circulation and calculate cardiac output from supplied data.

sow.alignment: Directly develops C32 through Pearson 8.7, 8.8 and 8.12. This LAUNCH exemplar adds named chambers, major vessels, pressure reasoning and calculations; it does not claim a wholly untouched topic or complete cardiovascular teaching.

priorLearning: Lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with blood.
A rate includes an amount and a time.
success: Trace the body–heart–lungs–heart–body route with named chambers and vessels.
Explain valves and the thicker left-ventricle wall using function.
Calculate output with correct units and state a limitation of the constructed data.

vocabulary.meaning: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart.
A vessel carrying blood towards the heart.
A heart chamber that receives returning blood.
A heart chamber that pumps blood out of the heart.
The volume pumped by a ventricle in one beat.
The volume pumped by a ventricle per minute: stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route, pen and ruler.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint; calculator where useful.
preparation: Print the shared page, one selected response route and the exit page. Routes are alternatives, not extra tasks.
Read the worked answers and note any constructed data before teaching.
safety: Paper and screen lesson; no human sampling, exercise test, breath holding, medicine handling or personal health disclosure.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied. Use paper diagrams and cards, pointing, annotation or dictation if a device is unavailable.

misconceptions.claim: An artery is defined as carrying oxygen-rich blood.
misconceptions.correction: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
misconceptions.check: Ask what makes the pulmonary artery an artery.

misconceptions.claim: The left ventricle pumps more blood per beat because its wall is thicker.
misconceptions.correction: In steady circulation the two sides have matching average outputs; the thicker wall generates the higher pressure needed for the systemic route.
misconceptions.check: Separate pressure from volume in the explanation.

misconceptions.correction: Muscle contraction creates pressure; valves open/close with pressure differences to prevent backflow.
misconceptions.check: Ask which structure supplies the pushing action.

misconceptions.claim: A fast heart rate alone proves greater output.
misconceptions.correction: Stroke volume matters too; output is the product of the two quantities.
misconceptions.check: Compare both columns before judging a pump record.

access.supported: Same core concepts with chunked prompts and read-aloud access. Record support used; a pathway is not a diagnosis or fixed attainment label.
access.standard: Explain the supplied evidence independently using accurate scientific terms and units.
access.stretch: Optional deeper transfer or evaluation. Higher-tier-only material is labelled explicitly and is not required for the core outcome.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner work, a quiet response, a pass and brief reset with clear re-entry. No forced disclosure or public performance.

slides.title: Can you design a route with no wrong turn?
body: Mission: follow blood through two linked circuits.
A correct route needs both destination and direction.
slides.notes: Use a finger trace or token. Explain that the diagram is a map of flow, not a scale picture of chest anatomy.

slides.title: Direction, exchange and rate
body: R1. Where does blood gain oxygen from air?
R2. What does a per-minute rate include?
R3. Does a larger pressure mean the same thing as a larger volume?
slides.notes: R1 lungs. R2 amount and time. R3 no; pressure and volume are different quantities. Accept everyday pump analogies with limits.

slides.title: Trace the full double circuit
body: Body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body.
Arteries go away; veins return towards the heart.
slides.notes: Think aloud around the loop, naming pulmonary artery and pulmonary veins as the oxygen-rule exceptions. “Away/towards” defines the vessel type, not oxygen content.

visual.title: Two linked circuits, one continuous route
visual.description: Schematic double circulation: body→right heart→lungs→left heart→body. Blue-labelled paths carry relatively oxygen-poor blood; red-labelled paths carry relatively oxygen-rich blood. Colour is accompanied by text. The positions are not anatomical.

elements.text: Two linked circuits, one continuous route
Artery = away from heart; vein = towards heart.

slides.title: Explain structure using its job
body: Atria receive; ventricles pump out.
The septum separates the two sides.
The left ventricle generates higher systemic pressure.
slides.notes: Trace atrium→ventricle on each side. A thicker left-ventricle wall supports greater pressure for the systemic circuit; do not claim it normally pumps a larger long-term volume than the right side.

visual.title: Atria receive; ventricles pump out
visual.description: Simplified four-chamber map. The body’s right side is shown on the left of the image. Blood passes from each atrium to its ventricle, with a septum separating sides. The thicker left-ventricle outline represents a thicker muscular wall, not a larger volume per beat.

elements.text: Body’s right is shown left; this is a structure model.

slides.title: Separate the pump from the valve
body: Muscle contraction changes pressure.
Valves open or close as pressure differences change.
They help prevent backflow.
slides.notes: Use forward and reverse pressure panels. Model output separately: 75 beats/min × 60 mL/beat = 4500 mL/min = 4.5 L/min. These are constructed examples, not a target for pupils.

visual.title: A valve permits forward flow and limits backflow
visual.description: Two-panel simplified valve model. Left: a forward pressure difference opens leaflets, permitting flow. Right: reverse pressure closes leaflets, opposing backflow. Valves do not provide the pumping energy.

Heart muscle creates pressure; valves direct the flow.

slides.title: Route engineering desk
body: W1. Match the four named vessels to their routes.
Add the missing atrium→ventricle steps.
slides.notes: Body→vena cava→RA→RV→pulmonary artery→lungs→pulmonary veins→LA→LV→aorta→body. Accept abbreviations only after names are understood.

slides.title: Pump data challenge
body: W2. Calculate output for P and Q.
Check both heart rate and stroke volume.
slides.notes: P: 80 × 55 = 4400 mL/min = 4.4 L/min. Q: 100 × 70 = 7000 mL/min = 7.0 L/min. Difference 2600 mL/min. No exercise test or individual health judgement is made.

table.caption: Constructed pump records; not pupil measurements.

slides.title: Repair the wall claim
body: W3. “The thicker left ventricle proves it always pumps more blood than the right.”
Replace volume with the relevant mechanism.
slides.notes: The thicker wall supports higher pressure for the body circuit. In stable circulation the two sides have matching average outputs, otherwise blood would accumulate in one circuit.
slides.reveal: Thicker muscle supports the higher pressure needed for the systemic route; it does not imply a permanently larger output.

slides.title: Which definition survives the lung route?
body: Choose the accurate statement.
slides.notes: First option correct. Re-trace pulmonary vessels if pupils classify by oxygen content.

options.text: The pulmonary artery is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart.
options.feedback: Direction defines an artery, even when its blood is relatively oxygen-poor.

options.text: Every vein must carry relatively oxygen-poor blood.
options.feedback: Pulmonary veins return relatively oxygen-rich blood from lungs to heart.

options.text: Valves supply the force that pumps blood.
options.feedback: Heart muscle creates pressure; valves help direct flow and prevent backflow.

slides.title: Produce a route-and-pump brief
body: Choose your response route.
Show the route, a structural reason and one calculation.
slides.notes: Use shared route/data page. Pointing with accurate spoken names is a valid access route.

slides.title: Make every arrow explain something
body: Name the vessel and direction.
Keep pressure, volume and rate distinct.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. If stuck, start from lungs→left atrium and build around the route.

slides.title: Audience checks the exception
body: L1. Share one vessel claim.
Audience asks: “Would it still work for the pulmonary vessels?”
slides.notes: Pupil corrects a definition or defends an accurate away/towards explanation. Quiet teacher/TA audience is sufficient.

slides.title: A route and a calculation need units
body: A correct name tells us where blood goes.
A correct unit tells us what the number measures.
slides.notes: Model 4.4 L/min as an output, not heart rate. Ask pupils to add one missing unit or destination.

slides.title: Three useful checks
body: E1. Which chamber pumps blood to the lungs?
E2. Why is the left-ventricle wall thicker?
E3. Calculate 60 mL/beat × 90 beats/min.
slides.notes: E1 right ventricle. E2 greater pressure for systemic circuit. E3 5400 mL/min = 5.4 L/min. Use errors to plan route versus rate re-teaching.

slides.title: Next useful step
body: Vessel direction • chamber route • pressure • output units.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. No comparison with a pupil’s pulse or health is required.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Route and pump records
pupilPages.intro: The route is a simplified adult circulation map. Pump numbers are constructed for learning.

blocks.text: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. 1 L = 1000 mL. Atria receive blood; ventricles pump blood out. The two sides are separated by the septum.

blocks.prompt: W1. Trace the route. W2. Calculate both outputs. W3. Repair: “The thicker left ventricle proves it always pumps more blood than the right.”

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Follow the blood
pupilPages.intro: Use the vessel table and calculator if needed.

blocks.prompt: S1. Complete a full route from body back to body, including lungs and the four chambers.
S2. Explain why the pulmonary artery is an artery even though its blood is relatively oxygen-poor.
S3. Calculate output for P and Q. Give one result in both mL/min and L/min.
S4. Explain one valve action and why the left-ventricle wall is thicker.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Route-and-pump explanation
pupilPages.intro: Use scientific names, mechanisms and units.

blocks.prompt: M1. Trace body→lungs→body through the named vessels and chambers. Explain the septum’s role.
M2. Explain how chamber-wall thickness and valves support the circulation, separating pressure from output.
M3. Calculate both constructed outputs and their difference, with units.
M4. Evaluate: “The faster pulse alone proves more blood is pumped each minute.” State what else is needed.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Test the pump interpretation
pupilPages.intro: Optional transfer. A constructed record R has 120 beats/min and 35 mL/beat. A record S has 70 beats/min and 70 mL/beat.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate both outputs. Which is greater? Explain why heart rate alone misleads.
T2. A faulty valve permits some backflow. Why might total chamber movement overestimate useful forward output?
T3. Explain why long-term unequal left/right outputs would be a problem for a linked circulation.
T4. A technician reports “5400 beats/min output”. Correct the quantity/unit error without diagnosing a person.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | A direction and a quantity
pupilPages.intro: Keep pressure, volume and time distinct.

blocks.prompt: E1. Which chamber pumps to the lungs?
E2. Explain the thicker left-ventricle wall using pressure.
E3. 60 mL/beat × 90 beats/min: show output and units.
L1. What did your audience ask? Improve one route or calculation label.

answers.label: Retrieval and We do
answers.answer: R1 lungs; R2 amount/time; R3 pressure differs from volume. W1 full route: body→vena cava→right atrium→right ventricle→pulmonary artery→lungs→pulmonary veins→left atrium→left ventricle→aorta→body. W2 P = 4400 mL/min; Q = 7000 mL/min. W3 thicker left wall supports higher pressure, not permanently larger output.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Pulmonary artery carries blood away from heart, so it is an artery. Pulmonary veins carry relatively oxygen-rich blood towards heart. Muscle supplies pumping pressure; valves direct flow.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: Use the full route above. Septum separates left and right sides, limiting mixing of the two streams in the normal adult heart.

answers.label: S2
answers.answer: An artery is defined by blood travelling away from the heart, not its oxygen content. The pulmonary artery runs from right ventricle towards lungs.

answers.label: S3 / M3
answers.answer: P: 80 × 55 = 4400 mL/min = 4.4 L/min. Q: 100 × 70 = 7000 mL/min = 7.0 L/min. Difference 2600 mL/min= 2.6 L/min.

answers.label: S4 / M2
answers.answer: Pressure differences open/close valve leaflets, preventing backflow. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to produce the higher pressure for systemic circulation. In stable circulation average outputs of the two sides match.

answers.label: M4 / T1
answers.answer: Need stroke volume too. R: 120 × 35 = 4200 mL/min; S: 70 × 70 = 4900 mL/min. S has lower heart rate but greater output because its stroke volume is much larger.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: Some moved blood returns backwards rather than progressing through the circuit; useful net forward flow can be lower than gross chamber movement.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: Because the circuits connect, persistently unequal average outputs would cause blood to accumulate in one part and deplete another. The thicker wall is primarily a pressure adaptation.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Output is a volume per time, so 5400 mL/min (if those were the measured volume data), not beats/min. Heart rate uses beats/min; a unit alone cannot diagnose health.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1 right ventricle. E2 higher systemic pressure. E3 60×90=5400 mL/min = 5.4 L/min. Secure core: route direction, pressure/valve mechanism and valid output units. Re-teach using away/towards if pulmonary vessels are misclassified.

teacherNotes: 40-minute lesson. Zero-minute slides share the preceding stage allocation.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing with explanation, annotations or writing; record the support used.
A teacher or TA can be a quiet audience: ask one evidence question, then let the pupil revise or justify a decision.
All pump data are constructed. This lesson requires no pulse-taking, exertion, health comparison or physiological threshold.
Interactive route/valve/data decisions use the same evidence as W1–W3. Manual progression and a paper finger-trace provide equivalent reasoning.
The heart diagrams are simplified flow/structure models with text labels as well as colour; they are not diagnostic anatomical images.
